System Proposal
EDUCATION SUCCESS OS
Development Plan
and Architecture Design
Integration-first intelligence and intervention platform for schools, colleges and universities
Core decision: build the decision-and-intervention layer first; expand into modular ERP replacement only after proving outcomes.
CONFIDENTIAL WORKING BLUEPRINT
1. Executive direction
Build one multi-tenant Education Success Operating System with configurable school, college and university packs. The first commercial product should integrate with existing ERPs, connect fragmented information, surface high-value risks and coordinate measurable interventions. It should not require an institution to replace its system of record during the pilot.
2. Product principles
Outcome before automation: each feature must improve a measurable institutional outcome or remove meaningful effort.
Configuration before forks: schools, colleges and universities share one platform and use different configuration packs.
Integration before replacement: respect the institution's current system of record.
Rules for facts, AI for interpretation: fees, eligibility, credits and permissions remain deterministic.
Human authority for sensitive decisions: grading, admissions, discipline, wellbeing and major financial decisions require accountable people.
Evidence before recommendation: every important recommendation includes source data, applicable policy and confidence.
Intervention before dashboard: risks become assigned actions with due dates, escalation and outcome measurement.
Privacy by design: least-privilege access, consent, auditability and data minimization are platform capabilities.
3. Product boundaries
4. Functional division by institution type
The platform uses shared services plus institution packs. Configuration controls hierarchy, academic structure, terminology, permissions, workflows and compliance obligations.
4.1 Configurable hierarchy and authorization
Do not equate job title with access. Model six independent concepts:
Role: user category such as teacher, faculty member, librarian, principal or registrar.
Position: the institution-defined job title.
Scope: campuses, departments, programmes, classes or students visible to the user.
Permission: operations the user may read, prepare, approve or execute.
Approval authority: monetary, academic or administrative thresholds.
Reporting relationship: who supervises, delegates to or escalates from whom.
4.2 Module catalogue
5. Recommended product architecture
Figure 1. The platform starts above existing systems and earns the right to replace weak modules.
5.1 Architecture objectives
Support multiple institutions with strict tenant isolation.
Connect to heterogeneous ERPs without embedding vendor-specific logic in product services.
Handle both structured records and unstructured policies or evidence.
Allow read-only pilots before enabling controlled write actions.
Separate authoritative calculation from probabilistic reasoning.
Provide explainability, human approval and immutable audit evidence.
Operate across web, mobile, low-bandwidth and approved messaging channels.
Scale by institution, campus and academic cycle without separate codebases.
Figure 2. Five-layer logical architecture with separation between user experience, intelligence and authoritative data.

6. Integration architecture
Every connector maps a source system into the canonical education model. Product services consume canonical records and events rather than vendor-specific schemas.
6.1 Read and write maturity
6.2 Canonical data domains
Organization: tenant, campus, department, programme, cohort and academic period.
People: student, guardian, employee, identity, relationship, role and scope.
Academics: curriculum, course, section, enrolment, timetable, attendance, assessment and result.
Finance: charge, concession, scholarship, invoice, payment, refund and balance.
Engagement: LMS activity, communication, mentoring, grievance and intervention.
Operations: library, hostel, transport, facility, inventory and service request.
Governance: policy, consent, approval, evidence, compliance control and audit event.
7. AI and decision-intelligence architecture
Figure 3. All AI requests pass through grounding, authorization, confirmation and outcome tracking.
7.1 Intelligence components
7.2 Model-development strategy
Do not train a foundation model from scratch. Start with a licence-approved multilingual open-weight model running on our GPU infrastructure, then build defensibility in institutional grounding, education data, risk taxonomies, workflow execution and intervention outcomes.
Phase A - Prompt and tool engineering: evaluate role-aware conversations using synthetic and de-identified scenarios.
Phase B - Institution-specific RAG: ingest approved documents with ownership, version, effective date and access metadata.
Phase C - Predictive baselines: begin with interpretable logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees, survival models and time-series forecasts.
Phase D - Domain adaptation only if justified: use LoRA/QLoRA on the selected open-weight model for intent classification, terminology or multilingual quality, using reviewed, de-identified and licence-approved examples only after the RAG baseline is measured.
Phase E - Outcome learning: use intervention and outcome history to improve next-best-action recommendations under governance.

The roadmap is organized by evidence gates rather than calendar alone. A phase closes only when its stated outcome is demonstrably achieved.

Library functionality is required for a complete platform, but it should not delay the intelligence MVP.
12. Delivery teams and ownership
12.1 Initial team shape
A focused first team is approximately 10-14 people: one product/domain lead, one architect, three backend/platform engineers, one data engineer, one ML engineer, one AI engineer, two frontend/mobile engineers, one designer, one QA engineer, one DevOps/SRE engineer and part-time security/privacy expertise.
13. Engineering standards
API-first services with versioned contracts and idempotent mutations.
Infrastructure as code and separate development, staging and production environments.
Automated unit, contract, integration, authorization and end-to-end tests.
Synthetic tenant datasets for development; production data prohibited from developer laptops.
Schema registry and data-contract tests for every connector.
Feature flags and tenant-specific rollout controls.
End-to-end observability for user request, retrieval, model/rule call, tool execution and outcome.
Documented rollback for model, prompt, rule, connector and application releases.
Accessibility and performance budgets treated as release gates.

18. Key architecture decisions to approve
Integration-first product entry versus immediate ERP replacement.
First pilot segment: school, college or university.
First design-partner ERP/vendor and available data-access method.
Primary first outcome: retention, admission conversion or accreditation readiness.
Cloud-hosted versus institution-specific deployment requirements.

Read-only pilot period and criteria for enabling write actions.
Commercial success metric and acceptable pilot duration.
19. Recommended next decision
Select one design-partner institution and one outcome. The recommended starting point is student retention for a college or university that can provide attendance, assessment, fee, LMS and mentoring data. Build a read-only Student 360, explainable risk model and intervention hub before expanding the ERP surface.
Appendix A. Suggested technology capabilities
Appendix B. Definition of done for the first pilot
No cross-tenant or unauthorized student-data access in the security test suite.
Every material answer cites a current authorized source or explicitly declines.
Every risk signal shows supporting data, prediction date and model/rule version.
Every intervention has an owner, due date, status, evidence and outcome.
Data totals reconcile with the ERP within agreed tolerances.
The institution can disable the model, connector or action without taking the portal offline.
Pilot leaders can quantify value, effort and safety compared with the baseline.
Engineering HLD
Education Success OS - Engineering High-Level Design
Architecture decision record for a 100,000-user, integration-first education platform
1. Architecture decisions
Decision 1 - Python is suitable for the backend and AI platform, but the complete system should not be Python-only. Use Python for APIs, domain services, integrations, background workers, data pipelines, machine learning and AI orchestration. Use TypeScript for the browser application because it provides the strongest modern web ecosystem, compile-time UI contracts and better client-side performance and maintainability.
Decision 2 - Divide the system into two deployment planes: Core Platform (non-AI) and AI/Decision Intelligence. They live in one monorepo, share contracts and platform libraries, but build into different images and deploy independently. AI failure must never make attendance, fees, cases, identity or other core workflows unavailable.
Decision 3 - A single physical machine is acceptable for local development, demonstration and an early pilot. It is not the production target for 100,000 users. Production must run the same containers across multiple nodes with load balancing, replicated state stores and failure isolation. “100,000 users” is treated as registered users; initial sizing assumes 10,000 daily active users, 2,000 peak concurrent sessions and approximately 500 sustained API requests/second with short bursts to 1,500 requests/second. These numbers must be replaced by measured pilot traffic before procurement.
Decision 4 - Begin as an integration and intelligence layer over existing ERPs. Every service owns its data and exposes contracts; services must not directly read another service’s tables. Use synchronous APIs for immediate commands and queries, and durable events for propagation and read models.
Decision 5 - Optimize retrieval with purpose-built stores: PostgreSQL for transactions, Redis for hot data and rate limiting, OpenSearch for lexical/hybrid search, pgvector for the first vector workload, object storage for documents and ClickHouse only when leadership analytics outgrow PostgreSQL read replicas/materialized views.
2. Quality attributes and design targets
Availability: Core Platform target 99.9% initially, evolving to 99.95%; AI plane can have a lower independent SLO without affecting core transactions.
Latency: p95 under 250 ms for cached reads, under 500 ms for ordinary core APIs, under 2 seconds for complex dashboards, and streamed first AI token under 3 seconds when the self-hosted inference service is healthy.
Scale: stateless services scale horizontally; no user session is stored in an application process.
Tenant isolation: every request carries tenant, user, role and scope claims; every datastore query enforces tenant boundaries.
Consistency: strong consistency for identity, finance state, permissions and workflow transitions; eventual consistency for search, analytics, notifications and AI indexes.
Auditability: immutable record of source data, policy version, rule/model version, recommendation, approval, tool call and outcome.
Recoverability: defined RPO/RTO, automated backups, point-in-time recovery and tested restoration.
Accessibility and low bandwidth: responsive PWA, incremental loading, compressed payloads, offline drafts and multilingual UI.
3. Recommended technology stack
3.1 Application languages and frameworks
Backend and AI: Python 3.14.x, pinned by service image. Use FastAPI for HTTP APIs, Pydantic v2 for contracts, SQLAlchemy 2.x plus psycopg 3 for PostgreSQL, Alembic for migrations and gRPC only for high-throughput internal calls that justify the added complexity.
Web portal: TypeScript 5.x, Next.js 16.2, React 19.x and Node.js 24 LTS. Use server rendering for fast initial pages, a client query cache for interactive screens and generated OpenAPI clients for end-to-end typing.
Mobile: launch as a responsive installable PWA. Add React Native only after usage data proves that device-specific capabilities or app-store distribution are necessary.
Data/ML: Polars or DuckDB for local analytical processing, scikit-learn and gradient-boosted trees for interpretable predictive baselines, and PyTorch only when a validated use case needs deep learning.
3.2 Data and retrieval
Transactional database: PostgreSQL 18 with PgBouncer, primary plus read replicas, PITR backups and tenant-aware composite indexes.
Cache/session/rate limits: Redis 8.x cluster. Cache only reconstructable data; never make Redis the sole store for authoritative records.
Event streaming: Apache Kafka 4.x for durable domain events, connector ingestion and analytics feeds. For a smaller pilot, start with a three-broker-compatible deployment or managed Kafka rather than embedding an in-process queue.
Search: OpenSearch 3.7 or the latest supported 3.x patch at implementation time. Use it for notices, policies, people/catalogue discovery, logs and hybrid lexical/vector retrieval.
Vector retrieval: PostgreSQL pgvector 0.8.x with HNSW for MVP knowledge bases. Move very large or specialized vector workloads to an independent vector service only after measured recall, latency and operating-cost evidence.
Object storage: S3-compatible storage for source documents, exports, evidence and immutable model artifacts. Store only metadata and object keys in PostgreSQL.
Analytics: begin with PostgreSQL read replicas and materialized views. Add ClickHouse when event volume and multi-dimensional leadership queries justify a columnar analytical store.
3.3 Workflow, deployment and operations
Durable workflows: Temporal with Python workers for long-running approvals, ERP synchronization, intervention SLAs and retryable cross-service orchestration.
Containerization: separate OCI images for each service. Docker Compose profiles for development/pilot; Kubernetes for production horizontal scaling and rolling deployments.
Gateway: Envoy, Kong or a cloud-managed API gateway for TLS termination, authentication integration, rate limits, routing and request IDs. Do not expose internal services directly.
Observability: OpenTelemetry instrumentation, Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards and centralized logs/traces. Define SLO alerts before production.
Secrets and keys: cloud KMS/Vault-compatible secret storage. Never put credentials in the monorepo or container image.
CI/CD: GitHub Actions or equivalent, security scanning, signed images, SBOMs, database migration gates and progressive deployments.
4. Deployment topology
Internet / Mobile / ERP Webhooks
|
CDN + WAF + Load Balancer
|
API Gateway
/           \
Core Platform     AI Platform
(Kubernetes ns)   (separate ns)
|                |
PostgreSQL/Redis   Model gateway + retrieval
\                /
Kafka + Temporal
|
PostgreSQL | OpenSearch | Object Storage
|
Analytics read models
On one machine, Core and AI use separate Compose profiles, networks, service accounts, CPU/memory limits and deployment commands. In production, use separate Kubernetes namespaces and node pools. AI workers may use GPU nodes; core services remain CPU-only. Network policies allow AI services to call only approved read APIs and controlled action tools, never core databases directly.
4.1 Single-machine pilot boundaries
Run reverse proxy, core services, AI services, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka-compatible broker, OpenSearch and object storage as separate containers.
Reserve CPU and memory for core services before allocating AI workers. Apply hard resource limits so embedding or model jobs cannot starve login or transactional APIs.
Use a dedicated self-hosted GPU inference machine during the pilot when shared-machine inference would exceed available memory, GPU capacity or Core isolation limits.
Back up PostgreSQL and object storage outside the machine. A backup on the same disk is not disaster recovery.
5. Monorepo and independent-service design
education-success-os/
apps/
web/                         # Next.js portal
services/core/
identity/ organization/ academic/
workflow_case/ integration/ notification/
document/ search_api/ audit/
services/ai/
ai_gateway/ knowledge_ingestion/ retrieval/ model_router/
embedding_service/ reranker/ inference_vllm/
risk_scoring/ recommendation/ evaluation/
packages/python/
contracts/ authz_sdk/ observability/ event_sdk/ testing/
packages/typescript/
api_client/ ui/ auth/ telemetry/
contracts/
openapi/ protobuf/ events/ jsonschema/
db/
migrations/ seeds/ local/
deploy/
compose/ kubernetes/ helm/ terraform/
tests/
contract/ integration/ performance/ security/
docs/
adr/ runbooks/ data_dictionary/
Use uv workspaces for Python and pnpm workspaces plus Turborepo for TypeScript. A root task runner provides lint, type-check, test, build and image commands. CI detects changed services but always runs contract compatibility tests for shared schemas.
5.1 Service rules
Each service has one bounded business capability, its own API, migrations, deployment image, health checks, SLO and owner.
Each service owns its database or PostgreSQL schema. Cross-service SQL joins are prohibited.
Public APIs use versioned REST/JSON. Internal synchronous calls use REST first; introduce gRPC only after profiling.
Publish domain events through an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change. A relay publishes to Kafka, preventing lost events.
Consumers are idempotent, store processed event IDs and tolerate replay and out-of-order delivery where the contract permits.
Shared packages contain infrastructure concerns and contracts, not domain business logic that couples services.
Deployments are independent: a new AI image, prompt or model cannot require a core-platform release.
6. Module and service catalogue
6.1 Core Platform - non-AI deployment
Identity Service: users, authentication federation, MFA state, sessions, service accounts and token revocation.
Organization and Authorization Service: tenants, campuses, departments, roles, positions, scopes, relationships, delegations and policy decisions.
Academic Profile Service: student/staff profiles, programmes, cohorts, enrolments and canonical academic references imported from ERP.
Integration Service: connectors, source mappings, sync jobs, webhooks, reconciliation, dead-letter handling and connector health.
Workflow and Case Service: interventions, tasks, approvals, SLAs, escalation, evidence, comments and outcomes.
Notification Service: templates, preferences, email/SMS/push/approved messaging channels, delivery receipts and digests.
Document and Policy Service: document metadata, versioning, access labels, effective dates, object-storage keys and evidence relationships.
Search API Service: authorized query facade over OpenSearch; applies tenant and scope filters before results leave the service.
Audit Service: append-only security, administrative and AI decision records with retention controls.
Reporting Read Service: precomputed role-specific summaries; never executes expensive multi-service joins on a user request.
6.2 AI and Decision Intelligence deployment
AI Gateway: model routing, prompt templates, token budgets, safety filters, response streaming and provider failover.
Agent Orchestrator: identity-aware intent routing, retrieval, rule/tool selection, confirmation requirements and action validation.
Knowledge Ingestion Service: virus scanning, parsing, chunking, metadata extraction, embedding, indexing and policy supersession.
Retrieval Service: hybrid lexical/vector retrieval, reranking, authorization filters, citations and retrieval-quality telemetry.
Risk Scoring Service: versioned features, batch/online inference, reason codes, calibration and drift monitoring.
Recommendation Service: next-best-action candidates constrained by policy, available resources and human approval.
Evaluation Service: offline test sets, groundedness, retrieval precision, language quality, bias checks and release gates.
AI Worker Pool: asynchronous ingestion, embeddings, batch scoring and evaluation; horizontally scalable and separately resource-limited.
7. Database high-level design
Use one PostgreSQL cluster for the pilot, but separate databases or schemas by service ownership. Every business table includes tenant_id, an ordered UUID/UUIDv7 primary key, created_at, updated_at, version for optimistic concurrency and source lineage when imported. Use row-level security as defense in depth, not as a substitute for service authorization.
7.1 Core entity groups
identity_db
users, external_identities, credentials, sessions, service_accounts
organization_db
tenants, campuses, org_units, positions, roles, permissions
role_bindings, scopes, relationships, delegations
academic_db
people, students, guardians, staff, programmes, courses, cohorts
enrolments, class_sections, attendance_facts, assessment_facts
integration_db
connectors, source_entities, id_mappings, sync_runs, sync_errors
workflow_db
cases, case_subjects, tasks, approvals, escalations
interventions, intervention_events, outcomes
notification_db
templates, preferences, messages, deliveries, digests
content_db
documents, document_versions, policies, chunks_metadata, evidence_links
audit_db
audit_events, access_events, ai_decisions, retention_holds
7.2 AI data structures
ai_control_db
model_registry, prompt_versions, tool_definitions, evaluations
conversations, turns, retrieval_runs, tool_runs, feedback
feature_db
feature_definitions, feature_snapshots, prediction_runs
predictions, explanations, drift_metrics
vector store
document_chunk_embeddings(tenant_id, policy_version_id, chunk_id, embedding)
search index
authorized denormalized documents with tenant/scope/effective-date fields
7.3 Indexing and partitioning
All high-volume indexes begin with tenant_id. Examples: (tenant_id, external_id), (tenant_id, student_id, event_time DESC), (tenant_id, status, due_at) and partial indexes for open/active records.
Partition append-only attendance, audit, notification delivery and integration event tables by month or academic period after measured size warrants it.
Use UUIDv7/time-ordered identifiers to reduce random B-tree writes and simplify event ordering.
Use GIN indexes for JSONB only on queried paths; promote frequently filtered fields into typed columns.
Use HNSW vector indexes per embedding model and tenant group where necessary. Evaluate recall against exact search before tuning for speed.
Use PgBouncer transaction pooling. Apply statement timeouts and separate connection pools for APIs, workers and analytics.
7.4 Data ownership and consistency
Source-of-truth ERP records retain source_system, source_key, source_version and last_synced_at.
Core services never overwrite authoritative ERP facts unless a configured write-back workflow is approved.
Search and reporting stores are rebuildable projections fed by domain events.
Delete/rectification workflows publish events so search, vectors, caches, object metadata and analytics are updated consistently.
8. Flow design
8.1 Authentication and authorized core request
User -> Gateway -> Identity verification -> Authorization decision
-> Target core service -> PostgreSQL transaction
-> Outbox event -> Kafka -> projections/notifications/audit
<- response with request_id and version
8.2 ERP synchronization
Scheduler/Webhook -> Integration Service -> staging validation
-> identity mapping -> canonical transformation -> service API/import command
-> transaction + outbox -> Kafka -> search/reporting projections
-> reconciliation totals -> connector health dashboard
-> retry or dead-letter queue on failure
8.3 AI answer with retrieval
User -> Gateway -> AI Gateway -> Agent Orchestrator
-> Core Authorization API
-> Retrieval Service (tenant + scope + effective-date filter)
-> Rule/Core read APIs for authoritative facts
-> LLM generation with citations
-> output validation and policy filter
-> streamed response + immutable AI decision audit
8.4 AI-assisted action
Recommendation -> autonomy policy -> prepare action
-> show evidence, impact and confirmation requirement
-> user confirms / approver approves
-> Orchestrator calls approved Core API with idempotency key
-> Core service validates again and commits
-> result validation -> audit -> intervention outcome tracking
8.5 Student-risk batch scoring
Scheduled Temporal workflow -> snapshot time-valid features
-> Risk Scoring Service -> prediction + reason codes
-> threshold and suppression rules -> create/update intervention case
-> assign owner and SLA -> notify staff
-> capture action and outcome -> monitoring/evaluation dataset
No LLM directly mutates databases. All actions go through ordinary core APIs, which repeat authorization, validation, idempotency and audit checks.
9. Capacity and performance design for 100,000 users
9.1 Workload assumptions
100,000 registered users across multiple tenants; 10,000 daily active users.
2,000 peak concurrent sessions; 500 sustained and 1,500 burst API requests/second.
Read-heavy profile of approximately 80% reads and 20% writes.
AI usage limited by role and budget: initially 20-50 concurrent generations, with retrieval traffic higher than generation traffic.
Seasonal spikes during admissions, results, attendance windows and fee deadlines require pre-scaling and queue protection.
9.2 Scaling controls
CDN caches static assets; gateway applies per-user, per-tenant and per-route rate limits.
Stateless API replicas autoscale on concurrency, p95 latency and CPU, not CPU alone.
Redis caches stable reference data and short-lived read models with event-driven invalidation.
PostgreSQL primary handles writes; read replicas serve safe read models. Slow dashboards are precomputed asynchronously.
Kafka partitions use tenant or aggregate keys to preserve ordering while allowing parallel consumers.
OpenSearch indexes are tenant-filtered and sharded by measured index size; avoid one index per small tenant.
AI requests use queues, concurrency limits, streaming responses, token budgets and circuit breakers. When AI is degraded, core workflows display a clear unavailable state instead of timing out.
9.3 Performance validation
Use k6 or Locust for API tests, OpenSearch Benchmark for search, pgbench/custom scenarios for PostgreSQL and end-to-end admission/result-day simulations.
Test steady state, burst, dependency slowdown, broker backlog, replica loss, GPU saturation and self-hosted inference-node failure.
Production sizing is approved only after measured p50/p95/p99 latency, saturation, error rate and cost per transaction are available.
10. Security and tenant isolation
Use OIDC/OAuth 2.1 federation, short-lived access tokens, refresh-token rotation and MFA for privileged roles.
Authorization combines RBAC, organizational scope, student/guardian relationship, purpose and delegated authority.
Encrypt data in transit and at rest; use separate keys or key contexts for sensitive tenants where required.
Mask sensitive fields in logs, traces, support tools and model context. Include only the minimum authorized personal data required for the use case, even though inference is self-hosted.
Apply WAF, input validation, malware scanning, egress allowlists, SSRF controls and prompt-injection defenses.
Store audit events append-only and export them to tamper-resistant storage.
Run dependency, container, IaC and secret scans in CI; generate an SBOM and sign production images.
Perform threat modeling and tenant-escape testing before every major authorization or connector change.
11. Reliability and operations
Core service readiness checks include required database and broker dependencies; liveness checks detect dead processes without causing restart loops.
Use timeouts, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers and bulkheads. Never retry a non-idempotent action without an idempotency key.
Define RPO/RTO per data class. Test PostgreSQL PITR, object restoration and search-index rebuilds.
Use blue/green or canary deployment for core APIs and model/prompt releases. Database migrations are backward compatible during rollout.
Maintain runbooks for ERP connector failure, GPU or model-serving outage, search degradation, queue backlog, tenant incident and data correction.
Key dashboards: golden signals, tenant traffic, connector freshness, database saturation, Kafka lag, workflow backlog, retrieval quality, GPU utilization, queue depth, tokens per second and AI infrastructure cost.
12. Implementation sequence
Phase 1 - Repository and platform foundation: monorepo, CI/CD, service template, identity, gateway, observability and local Compose profiles.
Phase 2 - Canonical data and integration: organization, academic profile, first ERP connector, mapping, reconciliation and outbox events.
Phase 3 - Core intervention workflow: case service, notifications, audit and reporting read model.
Phase 4 - Self-hosted knowledge and AI foundation: licence-approved model manifests, vLLM inference, self-hosted embeddings, document ingestion, hybrid retrieval, AI gateway, citations and evaluation harness.
Phase 5 - Retention intelligence: time-valid features, interpretable baseline model, reason codes and human review.
Phase 6 - Pilot hardening: load tests, tenant security tests, backups, runbooks, shadow mode and SLO acceptance.
Phase 7 - Production scaling: Kubernetes multi-node deployment, database replicas, OpenSearch cluster, broker HA and progressive rollout.
Phase 8 - Additional use cases: admissions intelligence, compliance evidence and selective ERP module replacement.
13. Decisions deliberately deferred
Dedicated vector database: defer until pgvector/OpenSearch cannot meet measured recall, latency or operating-cost targets.
ClickHouse: defer until analytics volume or latency justifies a separate analytical store.
Native mobile apps: defer until PWA analytics reveal a device-specific requirement.
Training a foundation model from scratch: do not include in the initial roadmap. Use a licence-approved open-weight model, RAG and optional LoRA/QLoRA adapters; reconsider pretraining only if future evidence establishes a unique data and economic advantage.
Service mesh: defer until service count and traffic-policy complexity justify the operational cost.
Cross-region active-active: defer until contractual availability and data-residency requirements are known.
14. Final recommendation
Build the backend and AI services in Python, but use TypeScript/Next.js for the user-facing portal. Keep Core and AI as separately deployable planes in one monorepo. Start on one machine only for development and pilot validation, with strict container isolation. Design every service as horizontally scalable from day one, and move production to a multi-node Kubernetes environment before claiming support for 100,000 users.
The fastest retrieval architecture is not one database for everything. Use PostgreSQL for correctness, Redis for hot data, OpenSearch for full-text and hybrid discovery, pgvector for controlled semantic retrieval, Kafka for asynchronous propagation and precomputed read models for dashboards. Add specialized stores only when measured workloads prove the need.

HLD & Business Flows
HLD and Business Flow Design
High-level architecture, stakeholder journeys and system boundaries
1. How to read this design
The HLD shows the system’s major actors, deployable planes, data boundaries and integration direction. It answers what the platform contains, who interacts with it and how the major parts depend on each other. The LLD tab separately explains service-level sequences, database ownership, states, retries and approval behavior.
2. Non-technical stakeholder flow
This business flow is intended for owners, principals, deans, teachers and implementation teams. It explains how the product converts fragmented institutional signals into coordinated human intervention.
Observe institutional signals
(attendance • grades • fees • wellbeing • library)
↓
Detect risk, opportunity or service need
↓
Explain evidence and recommend next-best action
↓
Human reviews, assigns owner and approves action
↓
Student / parent / teacher engagement
↓
Measure outcome, learn and improve policy
↺
Figure H1. Institutional success flow from observation to measured outcome.
3. System context
The Education Success OS sits between institutional users and existing systems. Existing ERP/LMS products remain authoritative during the integration-first stage; the new platform provides intelligence, coordination and outcome tracking.

Figure H2. System context and external actors.
4. Independently deployable Core and AI planes
Core Platform and AI Platform share contracts and a monorepo, but they run as separate deployments. The AI plane includes self-hosted embeddings, retrieval, model routing and vLLM GPU inference. It can fail, restart or scale without interrupting identity, synchronization, workflows, cases or audit operations.
CORE PLATFORM — independent deployment
Gateway | Identity | Tenant | Integration | Student | Academic
Attendance | Assessment | Workflow | Intervention | Library | Audit
│ APIs + versioned events
▼
AI PLATFORM — independent deployment
AI Gateway | Retrieval | Risk Scoring | Recommendations | Model Router
Agent Orchestrator | Guardrails | Evaluation | Model Registry | vLLM GPU Inference
Shared infrastructure: PostgreSQL • Redis • Event Bus • OpenSearch
Separate health checks, scaling, release pipelines and rollback.
Figure H3. High-level service and deployment planes.
5. Technical data movement
ERP and LMS data enters through controlled connectors, is validated and mapped into canonical domain commands, then produces durable events. Search, reporting and AI feature stores are rebuildable projections rather than alternate systems of record.
ERP / LMS / SIS / Library / Finance
↓
Connector adapters → Validation → Canonical commands
↓
Core domain services
↓
PostgreSQL + Outbox
↓
Event bus / asynchronous workers
↙             ↓              ↘
OpenSearch       Reporting store     AI features
↘             ↓              ↙
Dashboards • alerts • decisions
Figure H4. Technical data flow from source systems to decisions.
6. HLD boundary decisions
The web portal calls services only through the API gateway.
AI services access core information only through authorized APIs and event feeds, never by reading core databases directly.
Each core domain service owns its writes and publishes domain events with the outbox pattern.
PostgreSQL is authoritative for transactions; Redis, OpenSearch, vectors and reporting stores are reconstructable acceleration layers.
A single server is acceptable for development and pilot deployment. Production support for 100,000 registered users requires multiple application nodes and replicated stateful services.
LLD Technical Flows
LLD Technical Flow Design
Service sequences, state transitions, database ownership and operational behavior
1. Database ownership
Each service owns a database or PostgreSQL schema. Cross-service SQL joins are prohibited. Synchronous APIs and durable domain events are the supported boundaries; search, reporting and AI stores consume authorized projections.
Identity Service ───────→ identity_schema
Student Service ────────→ student_schema
Academic Service ───────→ academic_schema
Workflow Service ───────→ workflow_schema
Intervention Service ───→ intervention_schema
Library Service ────────→ library_schema
Integration Service ────→ integration_schema
Audit Service ──────────→ immutable_audit_schema
Owned writes → Outbox → Event Bus → Search / Reporting / AI projections
Rule: no service reads or writes another service’s schema directly.
Figure L1. Database ownership and read-model boundaries.
2. Grounded AI answer sequence
The orchestrator verifies identity and scope, retrieves authorized evidence, obtains authoritative facts from Core APIs and only then invokes the self-hosted model through the Model Router and vLLM inference service. The final answer is validated, cited and audited.
User → AI Gateway: question + session token
AI Gateway → Identity/Policy: authenticate, tenant and scope
AI Gateway → Orchestrator: normalized intent
Orchestrator → Retrieval: tenant-filtered semantic search
Orchestrator → Core APIs: current authoritative facts
Orchestrator → Guardrails: redact and validate context
Orchestrator → Model Router → vLLM GPU Inference: prompt + evidence + policy
Self-hosted model → Guardrails: draft answer
Guardrails → User: validated answer + citations
Orchestrator → Audit: sources, versions, latency and result
Figure L2. Detailed sequence for an AI answer with citations.
3. AI-assisted approved action sequence
The model cannot write to a database. It prepares a proposed action, shows evidence, obtains confirmation or approval, and calls an approved Core API. The Core service repeats authorization and validation before committing.
User → AI Gateway: request an action
AI Gateway → Orchestrator: identity + tenant + intent
Orchestrator → Retrieval/Core APIs: obtain authorized evidence
Orchestrator → Model Router → self-hosted vLLM model: draft proposed action; no write access
Model → User: proposal + evidence + expected impact
User/Approver → Orchestrator: confirm or reject
Orchestrator → Core API: signed command + idempotency key
Core API → Policy Engine: re-authorize and validate
Core API → PostgreSQL/Outbox: atomic commit + domain event
Audit Service ← all steps, tool calls and outcome
Figure L3. Detailed sequence for a confirmed AI-assisted action.
4. Intervention case state model
Risks are operational only when they become owned cases. The state model supports review, assignment, SLA escalation, evidence collection, outcome measurement and cancellation with a recorded reason.
DETECTED → TRIAGED → ASSIGNED → IN PROGRESS → RESOLVED → CLOSED
│           │          │             │              │
│           │          └─ SLA timer ─┴─ escalation ─┘
│           └─ reject / false positive → CANCELLED
└─ duplicate → link to existing case
Reopen: RESOLVED or CLOSED → ASSIGNED
Every transition records actor, time, reason, evidence and tenant.
Figure L4. Intervention state transitions and exception paths.
5. Service-level contracts
Every command includes tenant_id, actor_id, request_id and idempotency_key.
Every event includes event_id, event_type, aggregate_id, tenant_id, occurred_at, schema_version and trace_id.
Every AI decision records retrieved sources, policy version, model and prompt version, tool calls, confirmation and final result.
Authorization is evaluated again inside the target Core service; gateway authorization alone is insufficient.
Consumers persist processed event IDs so replay does not create duplicate state.
6. Failure and recovery behavior
Transient dependency failures use bounded retry with exponential backoff and jitter.
Permanent validation failures return structured error codes and are not retried automatically.
Failed integration events move to a dead-letter queue and appear in reconciliation reports.
If the Model Router, vLLM server, embedding service or GPU node is unavailable, Core Platform workflows remain usable and show a clear degraded-state message. Requests already queued receive a bounded retry or explicit failure; they never block Core threads.
Search and reporting indexes can be rebuilt from domain events without modifying source records.
Non-idempotent external actions require an idempotency key and stored provider response before retry.
ERP Migration & Integration Plan
ERP Migration & Integration Plan
Risk-complete playbook for cloud, on-premises, hybrid and file-based institutional systems
1. Purpose and recommended strategy
Use integration first, coexistence second and selective ERP replacement only after institutional approval. During discovery and pilot, the existing ERP remains authoritative. Education Success OS initially provides unified workflows, interventions, analytics and AI assistance. Record ownership moves only after reconciliation, acceptance and a signed cutover decision.
Guiding controls
No production cutover without a rehearsed rollback.
No direct AI write access to source or canonical databases.
No cross-tenant data movement.
No assumption that institutions using the same ERP share the same schema.
No silent data correction; every transformation is traceable.
No inbound firewall exposure for an on-premises connector by default.
No source retirement until retention, audit and legal obligations are satisfied.
2. Deployment and migration decision tree
If the ERP is SaaS with stable APIs, use API-based incremental synchronization and vendor webhooks.
If the ERP is SaaS with weak or rate-limited APIs, combine scheduled exports, incremental calls and reconciliation.
If the ERP runs locally, install a read-limited Institution Connector Agent inside the network. It initiates outbound encrypted connections and buffers data during outages.
If cloud transfer is prohibited, deploy Core and approved AI services on premises, or synchronize only de-identified projections.
If the institution keeps its ERP, use permanent coexistence and position Education Success OS as the intelligence and orchestration layer.
If the institution replaces its ERP, cut over by domain: identity and reference data, academics, attendance, assessment, fees, library and remaining modules.
If no database or API is accessible, ingest controlled CSV, Excel, XML or JSON exports through secure SFTP or a watched folder.
If records are partly paper-based, use controlled digitization with dual verification and exception queues.
3. Target integration architecture
Local or cloud systems feed source-specific adapters. Adapters send records through mapping and validation to canonical education commands. Domain services validate ownership and rules, write to their PostgreSQL schemas and publish durable outbox events. Search, reporting and AI stores are rebuildable projections.
Local ERP / database / export folder
→ Institution Connector Agent
→ encrypted outbound channel
→ Integration Gateway
→ staging and malware scan
→ schema mapping and validation
→ canonical commands
→ domain services and reconciliation
Connector controls
Use least-privilege, preferably read-only source accounts.
Store credentials in an operating-system or enterprise secrets vault.
Use mutual TLS, tenant-bound certificates and certificate rotation.
Persist checkpoints so synchronization resumes without duplication.
Encrypt the bounded local buffer and enforce retention limits.
Sign connector packages and support controlled update and rollback.
Monitor health, last sync, lag, rejected records and disk capacity.
Support an offline export package where continuous connectivity is forbidden.
4. Canonical education data model
Adapters understand individual ERP formats; Core services understand only the canonical model. Core entities include institution, campus, department, academic period, programme, course, section, student, guardian, employee, role, enrolment, timetable, attendance, assessment, grade, fee, payment, scholarship, library item, member, loan, reservation, fine, consent and intervention case.
Every canonical record carries tenant_id, source_system, source_record_id, source_version, effective_time, ingestion_time, correlation_id and data_classification. Sensitive attributes are classified and minimized.
Mappings are versioned per institution. Value translations, dates, timezones, currencies, code lists, defaults and calculations are testable configuration rather than hard-coded domain logic.
5. Migration phases and gates
Phase 0 — Sponsorship and scope
Confirm sponsor, owners, modules, campuses, regulations, success measures, downtime and decision authority.
Gate: signed scope and ownership matrix.
Phase 1 — Technical and data discovery
Inventory servers, operating systems, database engines and versions, network zones, modules, customizations, APIs, integrations, jobs, files, volumes, growth, peaks and retention.
Gate: approved source inventory, classification and connectivity decision.
Phase 2 — Data assessment
Measure completeness, uniqueness, validity, integrity, orphans, duplicates, encoding, dates and inconsistent codes. Identify the authoritative source for duplicated fields.
Gate: quality baseline and remediation owners.
Phase 3 — Mapping and connector design
Define source-to-canonical mapping, identity matching, deletion semantics, frequency and conflicts. Build adapter configuration and contract tests.
Gate: business and technical owner approval.
Phase 4 — Secure infrastructure
Install connector, secrets, certificates, firewall rules, monitoring and secure staging. Test connectivity, throughput and recovery.
Gate: security and infrastructure approval.
Phase 5 — Historical trial
Load a representative slice into non-production. Compare counts, financial totals, attendance, grades, library balances and sampled fields.
Gate: thresholds achieved and defects assigned.
Phase 6 — Incremental pilot
Test change capture, timestamp deltas, webhooks or scheduled extracts. Verify checkpoints, duplicate suppression, deletes, late and out-of-order events.
Gate: lag, accuracy and recovery targets achieved.
Phase 7 — Acceptance and rehearsal
Test institutional journeys with administrators, teachers, finance, librarians, students and parents. Rehearse support, restore, cutover and rollback.
Gate: business and operations sign-off.
Phase 8 — Production cutover
Freeze only required functions, run final delta, reconcile, enable approved target writes and monitor critical journeys through a command centre.
Gate: stabilization metrics met.
Phase 9 — Hypercare
Monitor defects, lag, queues, data quality, performance, adoption and support load. Resolve mapping exceptions before expansion.
Gate: steady-state service levels met.
Phase 10 — Selective decommissioning
Retire modules only after retention export, audit validation, dependency review, backup proof and written approval. Keep read-only archives when required.
Gate: decommission certificate and recovery evidence.
6. Database and format variations
Different database engine
Problem: SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB, proprietary stores or desktop databases.
Solution: engine-specific adapters behind one connector interface. Prefer vendor APIs; otherwise use supported drivers and read-only views. Normalize before domain services.
Fallback: signed scheduled exports with checksums and reconciliation.
Customized or unknown schema
Problem: custom tables, renamed columns and institution-specific modules.
Solution: schema discovery, representative profiling and owner-led mapping. Store mappings per tenant and version. Never infer meaning only from a column name.
Fallback: vendor-supported views or reports.
Legacy database version
Problem: unsupported drivers, encryption or change capture.
Solution: a compatible read-only connector runtime near the source transfers normalized encrypted batches to the modern gateway.
Fallback: periodic export and reconciliation.
Different encoding or language
Problem: legacy encodings and multiple scripts.
Solution: detect encoding, normalize Unicode carefully, retain original values for audit and test multilingual round-trips.
Fallback: quarantine unconvertible values; never replace silently.
Dates, timezones and calendars
Problem: ambiguous dates, local time, UTC, daylight-saving changes and custom academic periods.
Solution: retain source value; store effective time with timezone and explicit parsing/calendar rules.
Fallback: reject ambiguous records instead of guessing.
Different identifiers
Problem: admission number, roll number, email, government ID and historical IDs may refer to one person.
Solution: tenant-scoped master identity with source aliases, deterministic rules and scored human review.
Fallback: provisional identity and merge-review queue.
7. Synchronization and coexistence exceptions
No change-data capture
Use updated timestamps, increasing keys, audit tables or snapshot comparison. Store watermarks with overlap windows.
Unreliable timestamps
Use row hashes and snapshot differencing with source-version evidence.
API rate limits
Throttle, batch, back off with jitter and prioritize critical domains. Monitor quota and catch-up time.
Internet outage
Buffer encrypted bounded batches locally and resume from the last acknowledged checkpoint. Local ERP operations continue.
Source unavailable
Pause without advancing the checkpoint. Preserve the last consistent state and reconcile the missing interval after recovery.
Duplicate or replayed records
Use idempotency keys based on tenant, source, entity and version. Consumers persist processed event IDs.
Late or out-of-order records
Compare source version and effective time. Reject stale destructive changes or apply the domain conflict policy.
Deleted source record
Define per-entity behavior: soft delete, deactivate, anonymize, retain or ignore. Financial, academic and audit records normally require retention.
Two systems update the same field
Maintain a field-level authority matrix. Only the authoritative system writes; conflicts enter review.
Circular synchronization
Tag origin and correlation ID. Do not export a change back to its origin unless the contract requires acknowledgement.
8. Data quality and reconciliation
Validate files, batches, records and fields. Quarantine invalid records without blocking valid records unless atomic consistency is required.
Reconcile using counts, distinct IDs, financial sums, attendance totals, grade distributions, library items and balances, plus sampled field comparisons. Reports separate expected transformations from defects.
Financial balances normally require exact reconciliation. Identity, enrolment and current academic data require near-complete reconciliation with every exception explained. Historical optional data may use an approved tolerance.
Exception flow
Detected → classified → assigned → corrected at source or mapping → replayed → reconciled → closed.
Every override records actor, reason, evidence and approval.
9. Security, privacy and compliance
Excessive source access
Use least-privilege accounts, read-only views and field allowlists. Log connector queries and administration.
Unnecessary sensitive data
Minimize at extraction. Mask, tokenize or exclude health, disability, financial and government identifiers unless approved use requires them.
Credential compromise
Use short-lived credentials where possible, vault storage, rotation, tenant-bound certificates and immediate revocation. Never store secrets in mapping files or logs.
Data residency restriction
Use an approved region, on-premises deployment or approved projections. Record where backups, logs, vectors and model requests are processed.
Consent and purpose limitation
Migrate consent and preferences. Enforce tenant, purpose and role authorization at retrieval and action time.
Correction or deletion request
Use authoritative correction workflows, apply retention holds and retain non-personal audit proof where permitted.
Self-hosted AI deployment and data residency
Use a self-hosted model gateway with tenant policy, egress deny-by-default controls, private model endpoints, licence-approved open-weight models and redaction. Do not send model requests to externally billed AI APIs in normal operation, and do not train a shared model on tenant data by default.
Audit gap
Record extraction, transformation, approval, AI evidence, model/prompt version, tool calls, target result and reconciliation.
10. Performance and scale risks
Large historical volume
Partition by campus, academic period and domain; use resumable batches and controlled parallelism.
Peak impact on the ERP
Throttle reads, use replicas or reporting views and avoid admission, attendance and examination peaks.
Slow queries
Select required columns, use indexed watermarks and paginated reads. Obtain DBA approval before adding source indexes.
Backlog after outage
Prioritize critical domains, control catch-up rate and shed nonessential projections. Publish recovery estimates.
One lakh registered users
Capacity-test concurrent active users. Scale stateless services horizontally; use pooling, Redis, PostgreSQL replicas, OpenSearch, queue backpressure and independent AI workers.
AI latency or outage
Keep Core workflows available. Use timeouts, circuit breakers and clear degraded-state messaging. Never block attendance, fees, library or emergency communication on AI.
11. Testing strategy
Contract tests cover adapter and canonical schema versions.
Transformation tests cover nulls, codes, dates, multilingual text, large values and duplicate IDs.
Integration tests cover authentication, retries, checkpoints, event replay, dead-letter queues and authorization.
Reconciliation tests compare control totals and sampled records.
Security tests cover secrets, certificates, tenant isolation, log redaction and vulnerabilities.
Performance tests cover peak reads, bulk loads, backlog recovery, portal concurrency and AI isolation.
Resilience tests interrupt databases, networks, queues, storage, GPU inference nodes, model-serving containers and connectors.
User tests cover admissions, enrolment, timetable, attendance, assessment, fees, library, communication, intervention and reporting.
Rollback rehearsals prove return to the last stable mode.
12. Cutover models
Parallel run
Both systems operate temporarily; recommended for high-risk domains. Define one authoritative writer.
Phased domain cutover
Move modules separately and avoid attendance or assessment ownership changes during examinations.
Campus-by-campus
Useful for operationally independent campuses. Prevent reports from mixing partially migrated semantics.
Big bang
Use only for small, simple systems with proven rollback and explicit leadership acceptance.
Read-only intelligence launch
Lowest-risk start: synchronize data and enable dashboards/interventions while operational writes remain in the ERP.
13. Go/no-go and rollback
Proceed only when backups are verified, final delta completes, reconciliation passes, critical journeys pass, support and monitoring are active, decision makers are available, rollback is achievable, security approval is current and open defects are within approved limits.
Stop or roll back when financial totals differ unexplained, tenant isolation is uncertain, current identity/enrolment integrity fails, critical integrations are unavailable, source recovery is uncertain, severe performance degradation occurs, auditing is incomplete or the rollback window is at risk.
Rollback is domain-specific: disable target writes, preserve evidence, stop outbound sync, restore the previous authority matrix and replay only verified source changes. Do not automatically reverse financial or externally communicated actions without approval.
Maintain the cutover checkpoint, immutable manifest, mapping versions, batch hashes, backups, pending-message inventory and external-action list. After rollback, reconcile both systems and schedule a new rehearsal.
14. Vendor and organizational risks
Vendor refuses database access
Use licensed APIs, reporting views or exports. Include vendor lead time. Never bypass licensing or security.
Vendor changes API or schema
Version adapters and mappings, detect schema drift, run compatibility tests and temporarily support parallel versions.
No documentation
Combine profiling, interviews and observed reports. Require owner approval for uncertain mappings.
Key employee unavailable
Document credentials, customizations, mappings and runbooks; assign primary and backup owners.
Process changes mid-migration
Freeze critical decisions per release. Route new requirements through change control and regression testing.
Low user adoption
Provide role-based training, champions, sandbox practice, contextual help and adoption monitoring.
Conflicting definitions
Create a glossary and authority matrix for active student, attendance, outstanding fee and completion before reporting.
Budget or schedule pressure
Protect security, reconciliation and rollback gates. Reduce scope or historical depth instead of skipping controls.
15. AI-specific risks
Poor history may create misleading risk scores. Start with descriptive insights, evaluate subgroup performance and require human review before automation.
Documents may contain prompt injection, obsolete policy or unauthorized data. Apply authorization, scanning, metadata filters, citations and tool guardrails.
Model behavior can change. Version models, prompts, retrieval configuration and evaluation datasets; regress before promotion.
Do not train a general shared model on institutional data by default. Begin with retrieval-augmented generation, rules and conventional predictive models only for validated use cases. Training requires explicit purpose, lawful basis, representative data, de-identification where possible, evaluation, approval and monitoring.
16. Post-migration operating model
Integration operations own connector health, lag, rejected records, certificates, queues and vendor changes.
Data stewards own definitions, mappings, quality exceptions and reconciliation.
Security owns access reviews, incidents, secrets, residency and audit.
Domain owners approve authority changes and cutovers.
Platform operations own releases, backups, capacity, observability and disaster recovery.
AI governance owns approved use cases, evaluations, model changes and human-approval policy.
Define service objectives for connector availability, synchronization lag, record freshness, reconciliation completion, incident response, recovery time and recovery point per institution and domain.
17. Required migration deliverables
Approved scope and stakeholder matrix.
Source, interface and dependency inventory.
Data classification and residency assessment.
Source-to-canonical mapping specification.
Field-level authority and conflict matrix.
Connector installation and security runbook.
Data-quality baseline and remediation plan.
Test evidence and defect register.
Reconciliation reports and approval record.
Cutover, communication and go/no-go plan.
Rollback plan and rehearsal evidence.
Hypercare dashboard and escalation matrix.
Retention, archive and decommission plan.
Post-migration review and lessons learned.
18. Final acceptance criteria
Migration completes only when all in-scope data has an authoritative owner; reconciliation meets approved thresholds; exceptions have owners and deadlines; critical journeys pass; tenant and role authorization are verified; audit evidence is complete; backup and recovery pass; monitoring and support operate; users are trained; and the institution signs stabilization or decommissioning.
Commercial recommendation
Sell Education Success OS as integration-first. Institutions retain their ERP, adopt intelligence and workflow modules first, and replace individual ERP functions only after value, readiness and operational safety are proven.
Development System Design
Development System Design
Build-ready technical specification for the first production-capable release
1. Development objective and MVP boundary
Build an integration-first Education Success OS that operates over existing school, college and university ERPs. The first release must prove secure tenant isolation, canonical data ingestion, role-based portal access, student success workflows, library visibility, notifications, reporting and grounded AI assistance without requiring the institution to replace its ERP.
MVP outcomes
An institution can create a tenant, campuses, roles and scoped users.
An administrator can connect one ERP through API, database or controlled file import.
Students, guardians, employees, courses, sections and enrolments synchronize into canonical records.
Teachers and authorized staff can view permitted student context and create intervention cases.
Cases have owners, status, tasks, evidence, SLAs, escalation and outcomes.
Library items, members, loans, reservations and fines can synchronize or operate natively.
Students and parents receive role-appropriate portal views and approved notifications.
Policies and institutional documents can be searched and used by a citation-producing AI assistant.
AI failure does not interrupt any core transaction.
All administrative, integration and AI decisions are auditable.
Not in the first release
Full ERP replacement, payroll, advanced accounting, hostel and transport operations, native mobile applications, autonomous AI actions, custom deep-learning models, a dedicated vector database and cross-region active-active deployment are deferred unless a signed pilot requires them.
2. Runtime architecture
The repository contains two independently deployed planes.
Core Platform
Web portal, API gateway, identity, tenant and authorization, canonical academic data, integration, workflow and intervention, library, notification, document metadata, reporting and audit.
AI Platform
AI gateway, document ingestion, retrieval, agent orchestration, guardrails, evaluation, risk scoring and recommendation services.
Shared infrastructure
PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka-compatible event streaming, Temporal, OpenSearch, S3-compatible object storage, OpenTelemetry collection, Prometheus and Grafana.
Dependency rule
The portal calls only the API gateway. Core services own transactional data. AI services access approved Core APIs and authorized event projections; they never read or write Core schemas directly. Every mutating AI-assisted action requires an approved Core API and repeats authorization, validation, idempotency and audit checks.
3. Practical deployable units
Keep logical domains independent in code and data ownership. For the first pilot, reduce operational overhead by deploying related logical services together where appropriate, without sharing domain tables or internal business logic.
Pilot deployables
web: Next.js portal and PWA shell.
gateway: routing, authentication integration, rate limiting and request correlation.
core-api: identity, tenant, authorization, academic profile, library, workflow, notification configuration, document metadata and audit APIs as independently structured domain packages.
core-workers: outbox relay, notifications, scheduled read-model jobs and Temporal activities.
integration-api: connector registration, mappings, sync jobs, reconciliation and connector health.
integration-workers: extraction, validation, canonical transformation and replay.
ai-gateway: AI policy, sessions, request budgets, streaming and audit coordination.
ai-workers: ingestion, evaluation, scoring and recommendations. ai-inference: self-hosted embedding, optional reranker, model router and vLLM GPU inference, deployed and scaled independently from Core.
Split trigger
A logical service receives its own deployment when it needs independent scaling, release cadence, fault isolation, ownership or security policy. Contracts and database ownership must allow the split without changing clients.
4. Technology baseline
Backend and AI use Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, psycopg and Alembic. The portal uses TypeScript, Next.js and React. Use generated TypeScript clients from versioned OpenAPI specifications.
Use PostgreSQL for transactions and initial vector retrieval through pgvector; Redis for reconstructable cache, locks and rate limits; Kafka for durable events; Temporal for long-running workflows; OpenSearch for authorized full-text and hybrid search; and S3-compatible object storage for documents and artifacts.
Use uv workspaces for Python and pnpm workspaces with Turborepo for TypeScript. Pin exact versions in lock files and container images during repository bootstrap. Upgrade through automated compatibility tests, not floating production tags.
