Repository rules
Domain business logic cannot depend on FastAPI, Kafka or database adapters.
Shared packages contain contracts and infrastructure concerns, not cross-domain business rules.
Every deployable owns its Dockerfile, health checks, configuration schema and tests.
Every API and event change runs compatibility checks.
No service imports another service’s persistence layer.
6. Core domain design
Identity and tenancy
Owns users, federated identities, authentication methods, service accounts, sessions, token revocation, tenants, campuses and tenant configuration.
Authorization
Owns roles, permissions, organizational scopes, guardian-student relationships, delegations and policy decisions. Initial implementation uses application-level policy evaluation with tenant-scoped PostgreSQL records. Introduce a dedicated policy engine only when policy complexity requires it.
Academic profile
Owns canonical people, guardians, staff, programmes, courses, sections, academic periods and enrolments. ERP-owned facts retain source system, source key, source version and synchronization time.
Attendance and assessment
Owns normalized attendance events, assessment definitions, results and calculated summaries when included in pilot scope. Source ownership is configurable per institution.
Library
Owns library locations, catalogue metadata, copies, members, loans, renewals, reservations, fines, circulation policies and provider mappings. It can operate as a read model over an existing library system or become authoritative for institutions without one.
Intervention and workflow
Owns cases, risk signals, assignments, tasks, approvals, SLAs, escalations, evidence, comments and outcomes. Temporal manages long waits and retries; PostgreSQL remains authoritative for case state.
Integration
Owns connectors, credentials references, mappings, jobs, watermarks, batches, rejected records, reconciliation and dead-letter replay. It sends canonical commands to owning services instead of writing their schemas.
Documents and audit
Document metadata, versions, access labels and object keys are transactional. Files remain in object storage. Audit is append-only and records actor, tenant, request, source, policy/model versions and outcome.
Reporting
Consumes events into role-specific read models. User requests never execute unbounded joins across transactional schemas.
7. Database ownership and initial schemas
Use one PostgreSQL cluster during development and pilot with a separate schema and migration history per logical service. Use a distinct database role per deployable and deny cross-schema writes.
identity_schema
users, user_identities, auth_methods, sessions, service_accounts, token_revocations.
tenancy_schema
tenants, campuses, departments, tenant_settings.
authorization_schema
roles, permissions, role_bindings, relationship_scopes, delegations, policy_versions.
academic_schema
persons, students, guardians, employees, programmes, courses, sections, academic_periods, enrolments, source_aliases.
learning_schema
attendance_events, attendance_summaries, assessments, assessment_results, grading_schemes.
library_schema
libraries, catalogue_records, item_copies, members, loans, reservations, fines, circulation_policies, provider_aliases.
intervention_schema
signals, cases, case_assignments, tasks, approvals, evidence_links, comments, state_history, outcomes, sla_timers.
integration_schema
connectors, connector_credentials_refs, mapping_sets, mapping_versions, sync_jobs, watermarks, batches, staging_records, validation_errors, reconciliation_runs, dead_letters.
document_schema
documents, document_versions, access_labels, source_links, retention_policies.
audit_schema
audit_events, security_events, ai_decisions and export_manifests with append-only permissions.
reporting_schema
student_success_summary, case_work_queue, connector_freshness, library_summary and leadership_metrics.
ai_schema
knowledge_sources, chunks, embedding_versions, retrieval_evaluations, prompt_versions, model_policies, risk_model_versions, predictions and recommendation_feedback. AI schema contains authorized projections and AI metadata, not duplicate authoritative student records.
Required columns and indexes
All tenant data includes tenant_id. External records include source_system, source_record_id and source_version. Commands carry idempotency_key and request_id. Events carry event_id, aggregate_id, tenant_id, occurred_at, schema_version and trace_id. High-volume indexes begin with tenant_id. Use time-ordered identifiers, statement timeouts and separate pools for APIs, workers and reporting.
8. API contract standard
Expose versioned REST/JSON APIs under /api/v1. Generate OpenAPI in CI and publish immutable contract artifacts.
Request requirements
Bearer identity or service token.
X-Tenant-ID resolved and validated against token claims.
X-Request-ID propagated across services.
Idempotency-Key required for externally retried mutations.
Optimistic version or ETag for conflict-prone updates.
Response requirements
Stable error envelope containing code, message, request_id, details and retryable flag.
Pagination through opaque cursors.
UTC timestamps with explicit offset.
No sensitive field returned unless permission and purpose allow it.
Initial public endpoints
POST /api/v1/tenants
POST /api/v1/users/invitations
GET /api/v1/me
GET /api/v1/students and GET /api/v1/students/{id}
GET /api/v1/students/{id}/success-summary
GET and POST /api/v1/interventions
POST /api/v1/interventions/{id}/transitions
GET /api/v1/library/items
POST /api/v1/library/loans and POST /api/v1/library/returns
POST /api/v1/connectors
POST /api/v1/connectors/{id}/test
POST /api/v1/sync-jobs and GET /api/v1/reconciliation-runs/{id}
POST /api/v1/ai/answers with streamed output
POST /api/v1/ai/proposed-actions and POST /api/v1/ai/proposed-actions/{id}/confirm
9. Event contract standard
Publish state changes through an outbox in the same transaction. Relays publish to Kafka. Consumers are idempotent and persist processed event IDs.
Initial event families
tenant.created, user.invited, authorization.binding_changed.
person.upserted, enrolment.changed, attendance.recorded, assessment.result_changed.
library.loan_created, library.item_overdue, library.fine_changed.
intervention.case_created, intervention.case_transitioned, intervention.sla_breached.
connector.sync_started, connector.batch_validated, connector.sync_completed, connector.sync_failed.
document.version_published, audit.event_recorded.
Compatibility rules
Add optional fields without breaking existing consumers. Never reuse a field with new meaning. Breaking changes create a new event version. Contract tests verify old and new consumers during transition.
10. Critical runtime flows
Authenticated core request
Portal → Gateway → identity verification → authorization decision → Core domain → PostgreSQL transaction and outbox → response. Event relay later updates reporting, search, notification and audit projections.
Local ERP synchronization
Scheduler or webhook → Institution Connector Agent → encrypted batch → Integration Service → staging → validation → mapping version → canonical commands → owning Core APIs → outbox events → reconciliation. Failures are quarantined or moved to dead letter without advancing the committed watermark.
Grounded AI answer
Portal → Gateway → AI Gateway → authorization → tenant-filtered retrieval → approved Core read APIs → guardrails → model → citation and output validation → streamed response → immutable AI audit.
Approved AI action
AI prepares an action with evidence and impact. A user or approver confirms. The orchestrator calls the approved Core API with an idempotency key. Core repeats authorization and validation before commit.
11. Local-server connector design
Ship a signed Institution Connector Agent for Windows and Linux as a container or native service. The connector opens outbound TLS only. Plugins support REST, SOAP, SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SFTP and signed file exports.
Connector components
Source adapter with a read-only account.
Schema discovery and approved query/view configuration.
Mapping executor using a versioned mapping set.
Encrypted bounded spool for offline operation.
Checkpoint and acknowledgement manager.
Health and diagnostic exporter.
Remote configuration verifier; secrets remain local where required.
Signed updater with rollback.
Safety limits
Configurable rows, bytes, duration and concurrency per extraction.
Read-only transactions and source query timeouts.
No arbitrary remote SQL execution.
Field allowlist and local masking.
Checksum, batch signature and malware scanning for files.
Watermark advances only after durable acknowledgement.
12. Security model
Use OIDC/OAuth federation and MFA for privileged users. Short-lived access tokens carry tenant, user, role and scope identifiers. Authorization combines RBAC with campus/department scope, relationship, purpose and delegation.
Apply tenant filters in repositories and database policies for sensitive high-risk tables. Encrypt transport and storage, isolate service accounts, rotate secrets and restrict outbound destinations. Mask personal data in logs, traces, support tools and AI prompts. Scan uploads, dependencies, containers and infrastructure code. Produce SBOMs and sign production images.
Threat-model tenant escape, broken object authorization, connector compromise, malicious files, SSRF, webhook replay, prompt injection, excessive AI tool permissions and audit tampering before pilot launch.
13. AI implementation design
Start with retrieval-augmented generation, deterministic rules and interpretable predictive baselines. Do not train a foundation model.
Knowledge ingestion
Authorized document upload → malware scan → text extraction → classification and access labels → chunking → embedding → pgvector/OpenSearch indexes → evaluation sample.
Retrieval
Filter by tenant, scope, document status and effective date before ranking. Combine lexical and semantic scores. Return source identifiers and quoted evidence spans to the answer pipeline.
Risk scoring
Create time-valid feature snapshots from authorized events. Begin with rules and a calibrated tree-based baseline. Store model version, features timestamp, score, reason codes and decision threshold. Run in shadow mode before staff see recommendations.
Evaluation gates
Retrieval recall and citation correctness.
Answer groundedness, refusal and sensitive-data leakage.
Tool authorization and confirmation behavior.
Risk model discrimination, calibration and subgroup error analysis.
Cost, latency and provider-failure behavior.
14. Deployment profiles
Developer profile
Web, gateway, core, integration and AI containers; PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka-compatible broker, Temporal, OpenSearch and object storage. Seed data and mock ERP adapter included.
Pilot single-machine profile
Separate Core and AI networks, service accounts, Compose projects, CPU/memory limits and deployment commands. Core resources are reserved before AI. Backups leave the machine. Externally billed model APIs are prohibited in the normal production path. If shared-machine inference risks Core capacity, move the self-hosted model router, embedding service and vLLM inference server to a dedicated GPU machine while preserving the internal AI contract.
Production profile
Kubernetes with separate Core and AI namespaces, horizontal scaling, network policies, managed or highly available PostgreSQL, Redis, broker, OpenSearch and object storage. AI workers may use separate GPU nodes. Use rolling or canary releases and backward-compatible database migrations.
15. Observability and reliability
Every request and event carries a trace and request identifier. Export structured logs, metrics and traces through OpenTelemetry.
Required dashboards
API traffic, p50/p95/p99 latency and errors.
Authentication and authorization failures.
Database connections, locks, replication and slow queries.
Kafka consumer lag and dead letters.
Temporal workflow backlog and failures.
Connector freshness, rejected records and reconciliation status.
Search latency and indexing lag.
AI retrieval quality, input/output token volume, GPU utilization and memory, queue depth, tokens per second, refusal rate, inference latency and model-serving errors.
Tenant-level usage without exposing personal data.
Use timeouts, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers and bulkheads. Core remains usable when AI, search, messaging or an ERP connector is degraded. Define and test backup, restore, RPO and RTO before pilot cutover.
16. Testing architecture
Unit tests cover domain rules without infrastructure.
Contract tests cover OpenAPI, events and connector adapters.
Integration tests use disposable real dependencies where practical.
End-to-end tests cover administrator, teacher, librarian, student and parent journeys.
Security tests cover tenant isolation, authorization, secrets and malicious inputs.
Migration tests cover mappings, idempotency, late events, deletion and reconciliation.
AI evaluations run as release gates for prompts, retrieval and models.
Performance tests cover steady, burst, backlog and dependency-degradation scenarios.
Resilience tests interrupt databases, brokers, networks, search, GPU nodes, model routers and vLLM inference containers.
17. Engineering definition of done
A feature is complete only when domain rules, API/event contracts, migrations, authorization, tenant isolation, audit events, observability, tests, documentation and rollback behavior are implemented. It must pass linting, typing, unit, contract, integration, security and relevant performance checks. Database migrations must be backward compatible for rolling deployment. Every operationally significant feature includes a dashboard or runbook update.
18. Decisions required before coding business modules
Select the first pilot institution and its ERP integration mechanism.
Confirm first-release domains and source-of-truth ownership.
Choose the identity provider and notification providers.
Agree data residency, backup location, RPO and RTO.
Approve the first canonical data dictionary and mapping ownership.
Confirm whether the first library implementation is synchronized or native.
Define AI-approved use cases and prohibited data classes.
Replace workload assumptions with pilot estimates when available.
Development can begin immediately on repository foundation, service templates, local infrastructure, contract conventions and mock ERP fixtures while these institution-specific decisions are finalized.
Implementation Backlog
Implementation Backlog
Development sequence, sprint outcomes and acceptance gates
1. Delivery model
Use two-week sprints, trunk-based development, short-lived branches and automated deployments to a shared development environment. The plan assumes a focused team and delivers a pilot-capable release in approximately twelve to fourteen sprints. Change scope rather than removing security, tenant isolation, reconciliation or rollback gates.
Recommended initial team
One technical lead or architect.
Two to three Python backend engineers.
One TypeScript frontend engineer.
One integration/data engineer.
One AI/ML engineer, joining full-time after the Core foundation.
One QA automation engineer.
One platform/DevOps engineer, initially shared.
One product owner/business analyst with access to institutional subject-matter experts.
Part-time security, data-governance and UX support.
Delivery streams
Platform foundation.
Core domains and portal.
ERP integration and data migration.
Workflow, library and reporting.
AI and evaluation.
Quality, security, operations and pilot readiness.
2. Priority rules
P0 work blocks all dependent development or protects tenant/security/data correctness.
P1 work is required for the first institutional pilot.
P2 work improves usability, scale or additional use cases but can follow the pilot.
Build vertical slices. Each sprint should finish at least one user journey from portal through API, authorization, database, audit and automated tests. Avoid building every database first and every screen later.
3. Sprint 0 — Product and engineering inception
Objective
Remove decisions that would cause architectural rework and establish the working agreement.
Backlog
Confirm pilot institution, ERP/vendor contacts and integration method.
Approve MVP modules and explicitly deferred modules.
Define personas, tenant hierarchy, role hierarchy and student/guardian relationships.
Define first ten critical user journeys and their acceptance criteria.
Create system context, threat model and data-classification workshop outputs.
Approve source-of-truth and field-authority matrix.
Create canonical terminology and data-dictionary skeleton.
Choose identity, email/SMS and object storage components. Select licence-approved open-weight generation, embedding and optional reranker models; record their licences and checksums; and select the development GPU plus vLLM serving configuration.
Define environments, branching, release, incident and change-control process.
Create initial architecture decision records.
Exit gate
Product scope, authority matrix, pilot integration path, security constraints and Definition of Done are approved. Unknowns are recorded with owners and decision deadlines.
4. Sprint 1 — Monorepo and local platform
Objective
Every engineer can clone, start, test and observe the platform locally.
Backlog
Create uv and pnpm/Turborepo workspaces.
Create Python service and domain-package templates.
Create Next.js application shell and shared UI package.
Add PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka-compatible broker, Temporal, OpenSearch, object storage and telemetry through Compose. Add a separate self-hosted AI inference profile containing the model router, embedding service and vLLM GPU server.
Create Core and AI Compose profiles with separate networks and resource limits.
Create environment configuration validation and secrets placeholders.
Add lint, formatting, typing, unit-test and build commands at the repository root.
Add CI pipeline, dependency caching, security scanning and container builds.
Add OpenTelemetry, structured logging, request IDs and health/readiness endpoints.
Create seed framework and mock ERP fixtures.
Acceptance
A new developer starts the complete stack with one documented command.
CI blocks formatting, type, test, contract and secret-scan failures.
Core remains healthy when the AI profile is stopped.
A sample request is traceable from gateway to database and back.
5. Sprint 2 — Tenant, identity and authorization foundation
Objective
Create secure multi-tenant access before business data enters the system.
Backlog
Implement tenant, campus and department models.
Integrate development OIDC provider and token verification.
Implement user invitations, identity linking, session/revocation records and service accounts.
Implement roles, permissions, campus/department scope, guardian relationship and delegation model.
Create authorization middleware and repository tenant filters.
Create gateway routes, rate limits and request correlation.
Build login, tenant selection, unauthorized and profile screens.
Add audit records for login, invitation, role and configuration actions.
Create tenant-escape security test suite.
Acceptance
A user cannot query another tenant by changing URL, request body or identifier.
Every mutation records tenant, actor and request ID.
Role and scope changes take effect according to the documented token/cache policy.
Privileged roles require the configured stronger authentication policy.
6. Sprint 3 — Canonical academic model
Objective
Create the stable education data contracts consumed by every later module.
Backlog
Implement persons, students, guardians, employees, programmes, courses, sections, academic periods and enrolments.
Implement source aliases and master-identity matching foundations.
Create canonical import command contracts and idempotent upsert behavior.
Create OpenAPI specifications and generated TypeScript client.
Publish person and enrolment domain events through the outbox.
Build administrator list/detail pages with permission-aware fields.
Create data dictionary, validation rules and representative fixtures for school, college and university structures.
Acceptance
Repeated canonical commands do not duplicate records.
Every record is tenant-scoped and retains source lineage.
Breaking contract changes fail CI.
School, college and university fixtures can coexist without separate code branches.
7. Sprint 4 — Integration framework and mock connector
Objective
Prove the complete extraction-to-reconciliation pipeline before connecting a real ERP.
Backlog
Implement connector, mapping set, mapping version, job, watermark, batch and validation-error models.
Create adapter interface for API, database and file sources.
Build a mock ERP adapter with realistic bad and late records.
Implement staging, schema validation, mapping execution and canonical command dispatch.
Implement encrypted credential-reference handling.
Implement checkpoint acknowledgement, retries, dead letters and replay.
Create reconciliation counts and field-sample report.
Build connector registration, test, run-history and health screens.
Publish connector lifecycle events and dashboards.
Acceptance
A mock dataset synchronizes into canonical records and produces a reconciliation report.
Invalid records are quarantined without losing valid records.
A killed worker resumes without duplication or skipped committed data.
No integration component writes an academic domain table directly.
8. Sprint 5 — First real ERP connector
Objective
Synchronize representative pilot data safely from the institution’s environment.
Backlog
Complete source discovery and approved extraction design.
Implement the required REST, database or file adapter.
Create institution-specific versioned mapping configuration.
Install or package the Institution Connector Agent when the ERP is local.
Add read limits, query timeouts, local encrypted spool and health telemetry.
Run schema-drift and mapping contract tests.
Load a non-production historical sample.
Resolve identity, encoding, date, timezone and code-list exceptions.
Produce reconciliation report and remediation backlog.
Acceptance
Source administrators approve access and performance impact.
Sample reconciliation meets agreed thresholds or every exception has an owner.
Offline interruption, resume and credential rotation are demonstrated.
The connector cannot execute unapproved arbitrary source queries.
9. Sprint 6 — Intervention workflow vertical slice
Objective
Turn synchronized signals into owned, auditable human work.
Backlog
Implement case, assignment, task, evidence, comment, state history, outcome and SLA models.
Implement state transitions, validation, optimistic concurrency and idempotency.
Implement Temporal workflows for SLA timers, reminders and escalation.
Build staff work queue, case detail, assignment and transition screens.
Add manual case creation from a student profile.
Create notification events and audit records.
Create role rules for teacher, counsellor, principal/dean and administrator.
Acceptance
An authorized teacher creates a case, assigns it, adds evidence and resolves it.
Unauthorized roles cannot view or modify the case.
Duplicate transition requests do not duplicate state or notifications.
SLA breach is detected after restart and produces an escalation event.
10. Sprint 7 — Notification and reporting read models
Objective
Deliver timely communication and fast role-specific dashboards.
Backlog
Implement templates, preferences, channel policy, delivery attempts and receipts.
Integrate one development email provider and a provider abstraction for SMS/other channels.
Build event-driven student-success summary, work-queue, connector-freshness and leadership read models.
Create teacher, principal/dean, owner and administrator dashboards.
Implement cache rules and event-driven invalidation.
Add digest scheduling and delivery-failure handling.
Add accessibility, low-bandwidth and responsive portal checks.
Acceptance
Dashboards do not execute cross-service transactional joins on request.
Failed messages retry safely and appear in an operations queue.
Users receive only messages allowed by tenant policy and preferences.
Core dashboards meet the agreed pilot latency under representative load.
11. Sprint 8 — Library module
Objective
Close the identified functional gap with a module that supports synchronization or native operation.
Backlog
Implement libraries, catalogue records, copies, members, loans, renewals, reservations, fines and circulation policies.
Add provider aliases and library connector mapping contracts.
Implement item search, availability, issue, return, renew and reserve APIs.
Build librarian circulation screens and student/parent loan views.
Create overdue workflow and notifications.
Publish loan, overdue and fine events to reporting and intervention rules.
Implement conflict rules when an existing library system is authoritative.
Acceptance
A librarian completes issue, return, renewal and reservation journeys.
Concurrent issue attempts cannot loan the same copy twice.
Existing-system mode prevents unauthorized native write ownership.
Outstanding loans and fines reconcile with the source during pilot migration.
12. Sprint 9 — Document and knowledge foundation
Objective
Create an authorized institutional knowledge base before adding generative answers.
Backlog
Implement document metadata, versions, access labels, effective dates and retention records.
Add upload, malware scan, object storage and text extraction pipeline.
Implement chunking and provenance storage.
Index authorized text in OpenSearch and embeddings in pgvector.
Create tenant, scope, status and effective-date filters before ranking.
Build document administration, search and access-review screens.
Create retrieval evaluation dataset using approved pilot documents.
Acceptance
Users cannot retrieve chunks from unauthorized tenants or scopes.
Every search result identifies the source document and effective version.
Deletion or access-label changes remove or update search and vector projections.
Retrieval evaluation has agreed baseline recall and latency measurements.
13. Sprint 10 — Grounded AI assistant
Objective
Provide useful answers with citations while keeping all core functions independent.
Backlog
Implement AI gateway, tenant policy, quotas, sessions and streaming. Deploy the pinned open-weight model through the model router and vLLM; expose only an internal inference endpoint.
Implement retrieval orchestration and approved Core read tools.
Implement prompt templates, output schema validation, citation validation and refusal behavior.
Exclude unnecessary personal data before constructing the self-hosted model context.
Record model checksum, adapter version, prompt, retrieval sources, tool calls, latency, tokens, GPU/inference deployment and result in AI audit.
Build portal assistant with sources, feedback and clear unavailable state.
Create evaluation harness for groundedness, citation, leakage, injection and refusal.
Add provider timeout, circuit breaker and fallback behavior.
Acceptance
Answers cite only authorized evidence supplied to the model.
Prompt-injection test documents cannot expand tool or tenant access.
Stopping AI leaves all Core journeys operational.
A prompt, open-weight model, quantization, adapter, embedding model or inference configuration change cannot deploy without licence verification, checksum registration and evaluation regression results.
14. Sprint 11 — Rules and risk scoring in shadow mode
Objective
Generate explainable signals without allowing automated adverse action.
Backlog
Define approved pilot risk use case, outcomes and exclusions.
Create time-valid feature snapshots from event projections.
Implement deterministic rules and a simple interpretable baseline model.
Store version, feature time, score, threshold and reason codes.
Create suppression, duplicate-case and human-review policy.
Run historical backtest and subgroup error analysis.
Expose predictions only to an evaluation dashboard in shadow mode.
Capture reviewer feedback without changing model automatically.
Acceptance
No score uses data unavailable at the prediction time.
Every score has reason codes and model/policy version.
Performance, calibration and subgroup findings are documented.
Business and governance owners approve or reject progression from shadow mode.
15. Sprint 12 — Security, resilience and performance hardening
Objective
Prove that the pilot can fail safely and recover.
Backlog
Complete threat-model mitigations and penetration-test preparation.
Run tenant-isolation, broken-object authorization, webhook replay, SSRF, malicious file and prompt-injection tests.
Run database backup, point-in-time restore, object restore and projection rebuild exercises.
Run steady-state, burst, slow-dependency, broker-backlog, GPU-saturation, inference-queue and complete AI-outage load tests.
Tune indexes, pools, caching, queue partitions and worker concurrency from measurements.
Create SLO dashboards and alerts.
Write runbooks for connector, database, broker, search, notification, AI and tenant incidents.
Generate SBOMs and sign release images.
Acceptance
No open critical security defect.
Restore and rollback complete within approved objectives.
Core latency and error targets pass representative load.
AI saturation cannot starve Core resources.
Every alert has an owner and linked runbook.
16. Sprint 13 — Pilot migration and user acceptance
Objective
Operate the complete solution with approved pilot data and users before production cutover.
Backlog
Run historical trial and incremental synchronization.
Reconcile current identities, enrolments, library balances and selected academic data.
Create pilot users, roles and scoped permissions.
Execute administrator, teacher, librarian, student and parent acceptance journeys.
Train administrators, data stewards, support and pilot champions.
Rehearse cutover, rollback, incident and communication plans.
Run AI in approved scope and risk scoring in shadow mode.
Capture defects, adoption issues and operational metrics.
Acceptance
Reconciliation gates pass or exceptions are formally accepted.
Critical journeys pass with named business owners.
Cutover and rollback are rehearsed, timed and approved.
Support, escalation, monitoring and communication are operational.
17. Sprint 14 — Production cutover and hypercare
Objective
Move approved capabilities into production with controlled ownership.
Backlog
Apply the go/no-go checklist and freeze required source functions only.
Take final delta and verify control totals.
Enable target writes only for approved domains.
Monitor connector lag, queues, database, search, notifications, AI and user journeys through a command centre.
Hold daily defect and reconciliation review during hypercare.
Track adoption, support load, response times and data-quality exceptions.
Close or assign all residual exceptions.
Complete stabilization review and next-release prioritization.
Acceptance
No unexplained critical reconciliation difference.
Source-of-truth ownership matches the approved matrix.
Service levels remain stable through the agreed observation period.
The institution signs stabilization, extension or rollback decision.
18. Cross-cutting epics
Security and privacy
Tenant isolation, authorization, consent, masking, encryption, secret rotation, audit, retention and incident response are implemented continuously, not postponed to hardening.
Developer experience
One-command environment, realistic fixtures, fast tests, generated clients, stable local ports, migration tooling and troubleshooting documentation.
Observability
Every new service and important workflow includes logs, metrics, traces, dashboards and actionable alerts.
Data governance
Every canonical field has definition, owner, sensitivity, source authority, transformation and retention treatment.
Accessibility and performance
Keyboard navigation, readable contrast, responsive layouts, low-bandwidth behavior, pagination, incremental loading and query budgets are part of feature acceptance.

20. Environment and release strategy
Local
Synthetic data only. All dependencies run through Compose. Developers can run only Core or add AI profile.
Shared development
Automatic deployment after main passes. Resettable synthetic or masked data. Used for integration and UI review.
Test
Stable environment for automated end-to-end, security and migration tests. Provider sandboxes and representative volumes.
Pilot/UAT
Institution-approved data, restricted access and release-candidate images. Changes require migration and rollback evidence.
Production
Signed immutable images, controlled promotion, protected secrets, audited access, backups and progressive deployment.
Promotion path
The same image digest moves from test to pilot to production. Configuration changes are versioned and validated. Database changes use expand/migrate/contract sequencing. Core and AI release independently.
21. Pull-request and release gates
Pull request
Linked ticket and acceptance criteria.
Architecture or contract note when boundaries change.
Tests for new behavior and failure paths.
Authorization and tenant-scope review.
Migration and rollback impact.
Observability and documentation update.
No secrets or personal production data.
Release candidate
All required automated suites pass.
OpenAPI and event compatibility pass.
Database migrations tested against a production-like copy.
Vulnerability findings are within policy.
AI evaluation passes when AI artifacts change.
Runbooks and alerts exist for new operations.
Rollback is documented and, for high-risk changes, rehearsed.
22. Pilot success measures
Canonical synchronization completeness and freshness.
Reconciliation exceptions by severity and time to close.
Core API latency, error rate and availability.
Case assignment, SLA adherence and outcome completion.
Library circulation accuracy where in scope.
Notification delivery and failure rate.
Portal adoption by role and task completion.
AI citation correctness, groundedness, refusal and user feedback.
Security incidents and unauthorized-access test results.
Support tickets, resolution time and user satisfaction.
23. After the first pilot
Use measured traffic, GPU saturation and total operating cost to size production infrastructure. Keep self-hosted AI mandatory, but scale it independently through larger or additional GPU nodes. Add more ERP adapters through the same connector contract and expand modules in dependency order. Consider native mobile, ClickHouse or a dedicated vector database only when measured requirements justify their operational cost.
The first development action is Sprint 0 and Sprint 1 in parallel: finalize pilot decisions while the engineering team builds the monorepo, local platform, CI, service templates, telemetry and mock data. This creates progress without locking institution-specific assumptions into the architecture.
Self-Hosted AI Architecture
Self-Hosted AI Architecture and Model Strategy
Implementation decision for the Education Success OS
1. Executive decision
The platform shall use self-hosted open-weight models. Production workflows shall not depend on OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic or another externally billed model API. Core ERP services and the AI plane remain independently deployable within the monorepo. AI failure must never interrupt admissions, attendance, fees, examinations, library, identity or other core transactions.
“Free model” means that the selected model weights do not incur a per-token vendor charge under their licence. Infrastructure, electricity, GPU capacity, storage, observability, security and engineering still have costs. The exact model and licence must pass legal and security review before production use.
2. Build-versus-train decision
Do not train a general-purpose foundation model from scratch. That path requires a very large curated corpus, substantial multi-GPU compute, specialist research staff, repeated safety training and continuous evaluation. It provides poor commercial return for the initial product.
Build our proprietary Education AI Platform by combining:
Open-weight instruction model hosted on our GPU infrastructure.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over authorized institutional data.
Education-specific prompts, policies, tools and workflows.
Interpretable predictive models for dropout, attendance and intervention risk.
Evaluation datasets and optional parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapters.
Tenant isolation, authorization, audit and human approval controls.
The resulting product is proprietary because its data contracts, retrieval layer, decision rules, workflow integrations, evaluation assets and fine-tuned adapters belong to the platform, even though the foundation model is open-weight.
3. Model selection policy
Start with an Apache-2.0-compatible 7B–14B instruction model that supports commercial self-deployment, structured output and the required languages. Candidate families may include Qwen or Mistral/Ministral, but selection is benchmark-driven and not permanently coupled to one vendor.
The production model registry must record model ID, exact weight checksum, source, licence, quantization, tokenizer, context limit, safety configuration, deployment date, evaluation result and rollback version. Never download model weights dynamically in production.
Selection gates:
Commercial-use licence approved by legal review.
Runs within the pilot GPU memory budget.
Meets accuracy thresholds on our education evaluation set.
Supports English and required Indian languages adequately.
Produces reliable structured JSON and tool calls.
Passes privacy, prompt-injection, harmful-content and tenant-isolation testing.
Meets p95 latency and concurrency targets under load.
4. AI deployment topology
Portal -> API Gateway -> AI Gateway -> Agent Orchestrator
-> Authorization API
-> Retrieval Service -> pgvector/OpenSearch
-> Approved Core read/action APIs
-> Self-Hosted Model Router
-> vLLM Inference Server
-> GPU + versioned model weights
-> Output validation and policy engine
-> Audit and evaluation pipeline
Deploy the following as separate containers or services:
AI Gateway: authentication context, quotas, request validation and streaming.
Agent Orchestrator: prompt assembly, tool selection, workflow state and citations.
Retrieval Service: authorized hybrid search and context construction.
Model Router: model/version selection, concurrency control and fallback.
Inference Server: vLLM-hosted generation on GPU nodes.
Embedding Service: self-hosted embedding model for document and query vectors.
Reranker Service: optional self-hosted cross-encoder for improved relevance.
Model Registry: approved artifacts, checksums, licences and deployment metadata.
Evaluation Service: offline test suites, online quality signals and regression gates.
Risk Scoring Service: separate classical ML service for interpretable predictions.
No AI service may directly read a core service database. It must use tenant-scoped retrieval indexes or approved core APIs. No model may directly mutate any database. Actions pass through authorization, confirmation, validation, idempotency and audit in ordinary Core APIs.
5. Pilot server configuration for 500 registered users
Assume 50–150 monthly AI users, 5–10 normal simultaneous generations and short peaks up to 20 queued requests. Confirm these assumptions through a pilot load test.
Recommended dedicated AI node:
One NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB VRAM minimum for a quantized 7B–14B model; 48 GB VRAM is preferred for higher concurrency, longer context or a larger model.
16–32 physical CPU cores.
128 GB system RAM.
2 TB enterprise NVMe storage for weights, indexes, caches and logs.
Ubuntu LTS with NVIDIA drivers and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.
10 Gbps internal networking where the AI and data nodes are separate.
UPS and redundant power for on-premises deployment.
If Core and AI initially share one physical machine, reserve CPU, RAM and I/O for Core first; place strict GPU/CPU/memory limits on AI containers. Production should move AI inference to a dedicated GPU node before usage grows. The architecture must also support a second warm inference node for maintenance and failure recovery.
6. Serving and performance controls
Use vLLM for model serving, streaming and continuous batching. Expose an internal OpenAI-compatible endpoint only as a protocol convenience; it does not call OpenAI externally.
Apply per-tenant and per-role quotas, maximum input/context/output tokens, bounded queues, request timeouts and cancellation. Cache safe, repeated, non-personal results. Use prefix caching where applicable. Protect Core APIs with bulkheads so GPU saturation cannot consume transactional resources.
Initial service targets:
Streamed first token p95 under 3 seconds at approved pilot concurrency.
Interactive answer completion p95 under 15 seconds for normal requests.
Queue wait p95 under 5 seconds under expected load.
Zero cross-tenant retrieval results in automated security tests.
Core workflows remain available during total AI-plane failure.
7. RAG and institutional-data flow
Document or ERP event -> ingestion queue -> malware and format validation -> text extraction -> classification -> access-label assignment -> chunking -> self-hosted embedding -> vector/index write -> reconciliation and audit.
User question -> identity and authorization -> query classification -> authorized lexical/vector retrieval -> optional reranking -> fetch authoritative ERP facts through Core APIs -> assemble minimal context -> self-hosted generation -> citation verification -> output policy validation -> response and immutable audit record.
Use RAG for changing or private facts: student records, attendance, marks, fees, timetables, library records, policies, circulars and regulations. Never fine-tune personal student data into a shared foundation model or adapter.
8. Fine-tuning strategy
Begin without fine-tuning. Establish a strong prompt-and-RAG baseline and collect evaluation evidence first. Fine-tune only when a repeatable failure cannot be solved reliably through retrieval, tools, schemas or prompting.
Permitted fine-tuning targets:
Education terminology and intent classification.
Reliable structured reports and JSON schemas.
Tool-selection and workflow-routing behaviour.
Institution-approved response style.
De-identified intervention classification examples.
Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as LoRA/QLoRA rather than full-model training for the pilot. Maintain dataset lineage, consent/legal basis, de-identification records, train/validation/test separation, model-card updates and rollback artifacts. A model cannot be promoted solely because its training loss improved; it must pass the production evaluation suite.
9. Predictive models versus language models
Do not use the LLM as the primary student-risk score. Build separate interpretable models using scikit-learn or gradient-boosted trees for attendance risk, dropout risk, fee-risk and intervention prioritization. Use time-valid features, avoid future-data leakage, measure performance across relevant groups and return reason codes.
The LLM may explain an approved risk result, summarize evidence and help staff prepare an intervention. It must not invent a score, diagnose a student or take punitive action. Human review is mandatory for consequential recommendations.
10. Data and model database structures
model_registry(model_id, name, family, version, source_uri, licence, checksum, quantization, tokenizer, context_limit, status, approved_by, approved_at)
model_deployment(deployment_id, model_id, environment, endpoint, gpu_node, configuration_json, started_at, ended_at, rollback_deployment_id)
prompt_template(prompt_id, use_case, version, template, schema_version, status, approved_by)
knowledge_document(document_id, tenant_id, source_system, source_key, classification, access_scope, version, object_key, effective_from, effective_to)
document_chunk(chunk_id, tenant_id, document_id, ordinal, text_hash, access_scope, embedding_model_id)
document_embedding(chunk_id, embedding_model_id, embedding, created_at)
ai_request(request_id, tenant_id, user_id, use_case, model_deployment_id, prompt_version, input_tokens, output_tokens, latency_ms, status, created_at)
ai_retrieval(request_id, chunk_id, rank, score, authorization_decision_id)
ai_response(response_id, request_id, citation_status, policy_result, user_feedback, retained_until)
evaluation_case(case_id, use_case, dataset_version, input_ref, expected_ref, sensitivity_label)
evaluation_run(run_id, model_id, prompt_version, dataset_version, metrics_json, gate_result, executed_at)
training_dataset(dataset_id, purpose, version, lineage, deidentification_status, licence_status, approved_by)
adapter_registry(adapter_id, base_model_id, dataset_id, method, version, checksum, evaluation_run_id, status)
Store sensitive prompt and response bodies only when explicitly required and allowed by retention policy. Prefer hashes, references and redacted audit fields. All AI records carry tenant ID, model version, prompt version and authorization evidence.
11. Monorepo changes
Add the following structure:
services/ai/ai_gateway/
services/ai/agent_orchestrator/
services/ai/retrieval/
services/ai/model_router/
services/ai/embedding_service/
services/ai/reranker/
services/ai/evaluation/
services/ai/risk_scoring/
packages/python/model_contracts/
models/manifests/
models/adapters/
evaluation/datasets/
evaluation/golden_tests/
deploy/compose/ai-self-hosted.yml
deploy/kubernetes/ai/
deploy/helm/ai-inference/
docs/model_cards/
docs/ai_runbooks/
Do not commit large model weights, training datasets, secrets or personal data to Git. Store weights and datasets in protected object storage or an internal artifact registry. Commit only manifests, checksums, schemas, configurations and reproducible training/evaluation code.
12. Development sequence
Phase A — Establish AI contracts, threat model, licence checklist, evaluation framework and representative de-identified test cases.
Phase B — Deploy a candidate 7B–14B model through vLLM on the target GPU and benchmark latency, throughput, memory and output quality.
Phase C — Implement self-hosted embeddings, ingestion, pgvector/OpenSearch retrieval, citations and tenant-scoped authorization tests.
Phase D — Implement the AI Gateway, orchestration, output validation, quotas, streaming, audit and Core read tools.
Phase E — Implement interpretable risk baselines in shadow mode; validate reason codes, calibration, fairness and staff usefulness.
Phase F — Run security, prompt-injection, privacy, failover and load tests at 5, 10 and 20 simultaneous generations.
Phase G — Pilot with selected roles, measure unanswered questions and unsafe/incorrect outputs, and tune retrieval and prompts.
Phase H — Fine-tune a small adapter only if evaluation data demonstrates a persistent, high-value gap.
13. Acceptance criteria before production
No external model API traffic is required for normal operation.
Model and embedding weights are pinned, checksummed and licence-approved.
All retrieval is tenant- and role-scoped before context reaches the model.
AI outage does not affect Core availability or data correctness.
Every answer identifies model, prompt and source versions in audit records.
Consequential actions require Core authorization and human confirmation.
Golden-set quality, hallucination, citation, latency and security thresholds pass.
Backup, restore, model rollback and GPU-node failure runbooks are tested.
Operational dashboards report GPU memory, utilization, queue depth, tokens/second, first-token latency, request failures and retrieval quality.
14. Cost model
There is no third-party per-token API charge for normal operation. Track total cost of ownership instead: GPU purchase or rental, server depreciation, electricity, cooling, rack/hosting, storage, backups, monitoring, engineering, security and model maintenance.
Calculate monthly AI cost per active user as:
(monthly infrastructure depreciation or rental + electricity/hosting + AI operations labour + storage/backup) / monthly active AI users.
Keep the AI platform independently deployable so a tenant can run it on institutional premises, in our managed private cloud or on a dedicated hosted GPU without changing Core service contracts.

[TABLE 8]
Stage | Allowed behavior | Exit gate
0 - Observe | Import data and produce quality reports | Identity matching and reconciliation meet agreed accuracy.
1 - Explain | Answer questions and cite data/policies | Grounded-answer and authorization tests pass.
2 - Prepare | Draft forms, cases and messages | Human reviewers accept quality and audit trail.
3 - Confirmed action | Execute low-risk action after confirmation | Idempotency, rollback and validation proven.
4 - Policy automation | Run approved routine actions automatically | Formal policy, monitoring and exception path established.
[TABLE 9]
Component | Responsibilities | Must not do
Language model | Intent understanding, explanation, drafting, summarization and tool selection | Calculate authoritative fees, eligibility or permissions from memory
RAG | Retrieve current policies, notices, manuals, curriculum and evidence | Use superseded documents without warning
Rule engine | Attendance, credits, fees, promotion, approval authority and eligibility | Generate subjective student or staff judgments
Predictive models | Retention, academic, fee, admission and demand risks | Treat probability as fact or determine punitive action
Optimization | Timetable, rooms, routes, workload and allocation | Override approved constraints or human authority
Workflow engine | Cases, tasks, approvals, SLAs, reminders and escalation | Execute sensitive actions without required confirmation
[TABLE 10]
Step | Deliverable | Quality gate
Define outcome | Precise label and prediction horizon | Business owner signs definition.
Assemble features | Time-valid, permission-approved signals | No prohibited or future information.
Normalize | Canonical features across ERP vendors | Data-quality thresholds met.
Train | Baseline and challenger models | Time-based train/validation/test split.
Explain | Reason codes and supporting evidence | Explanation matches model behavior.
Pilot | Human-reviewed recommendations | False positives and subgroup performance accepted.
Monitor | Drift, calibration and outcome dashboards | Rollback and retraining triggers defined.
[TABLE 11]
Control area | Required design
Tenant isolation | Separate tenant keys and access boundaries; tenant-scoped queries by default.
Authorization | RBAC plus scope and relationship-aware checks at API and tool layers.
Sensitive fields | Field-level encryption, masking and purpose-limited access.
Consent | Capture guardian/student consent, purpose, expiry and withdrawal where applicable.
Audit | Record input, retrieved evidence, rule/model version, recommendation, approval, action and result.
AI safety | Prompt-injection defenses, tool allowlists, output validation and citation requirements.
Human authority | Mandatory review for grades, admission, discipline, wellbeing, disability and major finance.
Retention | Configurable retention schedules and secure deletion workflows.
Incident response | Detection, containment, notification, recovery and post-incident review.

13. Compliance intelligence | Months 10-14 | Map evidence, detect gaps and coordinate corrective actions. | Preparation effort and missing-evidence rate improve.
14. Platform expansion | Month 13+ | Add connectors, institution packs, optional modules and confirmed write actions. | Repeatable implementation and sales economics demonstrated.

[TABLE 20]
Risk | Mitigation
Poor source data | Begin with data profiling, reconciliation and visible quality scores.
ERP vendor blocks integration | Use customer-authorized exports, standard contracts and alternate read-only adapters.
AI appears impressive but lacks ROI | Tie each workflow to baseline and outcome metrics.
False or biased risk signals | Use interpretable baselines, human review, subgroup evaluation and appeal paths.
Institution expects full ERP immediately | Maintain a published scope boundary and modular product roadmap.
Policy answer becomes outdated | Require effective dates, owners, supersession links and review workflows.
Staff resist additional work | Design the intervention flow inside existing responsibilities and measure time saved.
Security review delays launch | Complete threat model, data-flow inventory and controls before production data.
